item.title: Impulsivity in Borderline Personality Disorder
item.description:
Self-Control

Impulsivity in Borderline Personality Disorder

How learned beliefs shape and sustain self-defeating behaviors

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Impulsivity is a core feature of borderline personality disorder.
  • Impulsive behavior is often rewarding in the short-term.
  • Thoughts about ourselves can increase the likelihood of behaving impulsively.
  • Small "behavioral experiments" can provide real evidence that alternative coping is possible.

A couple weeks ago, a client was telling me about a big work project she had due soon. When I asked how it was coming along, she matter-of-factly told me “I haven’t started; I need the adrenaline of the last minute to focus.” To my client, procrastination was inevitable - a tendency she just had to accept about herself.

Over the years, I've heard many versions of this same story from the people with borderline personality disorder (BPD) I work with. The narratives they tell themselves – "I'm going to screw it up anyway, so I might as well quit now" or "I can't stand this feeling" – sound like observations about reality. But they're actually interpretations that have been repeated so many times they feel like facts.

The more certain you are that you’re "the kind of person" who needs the pressure of the last minute, quits when things get hard, or can't tolerate emotional pain, the more likely you are to behave accordingly.

Impulsivity Is More Than Acting Without Thinking

When most people think about impulsivity in BPD, they imagine dramatic behaviors like reckless spending, substance use, unsafe sex, or self-harm. While these certainly can be expressions of impulsivity, they represent only part of the picture. Research suggests that it is useful to think about impulsivity as showing up in four distinct but related ways.

Some people struggle with planning ahead. They repeatedly put off important tasks because they tell themselves they work better under pressure. This can look like procrastinating on a project, waiting until the last minute to pack, or even failing to keep track of your commitments.

Others struggle with following through; they begin projects, relationships, or goals with enthusiasm but abandon them as soon as they hit a setback. This could look like ordering take-out when you committed to cooking at home because you had a hard day, or giving up on sobriety because you had one drink.

Others act impulsively in response to intense emotions, desperately trying to escape emotional pain. This is what we usually think of when we picture impulsivity in BPD.

Still others seek out novelty and excitement, hoping to cut through feelings of emptiness or numbness. This could look like driving fast, using substances, or even just skipping out on work to go to the beach.

Although these behaviors look very different, they are driven by similar processes.

How Impulsive Behaviors Become Part of Our Identity

People with BPD often have a biological predisposition to experience emotions more intensely and to be especially sensitive to immediate rewards. But biology is only part of the story. The explanations we give ourselves for our behavior also determine the likelihood we’ll repeat them.

article continues after advertisement

Take procrastination: Imagine you delay working on an important presentation because thinking about it makes you anxious. The moment you give yourself permission to put it off until tomorrow, you’ll likely feel relieved. Your behavior reinforced the idea that you can’t handle stress - why else would you have avoided working on the project? Days later, with the deadline looming, you mistake the panic you’re feeling for “adrenaline” and conclude “I’m the type of person who needs pressure to get work done.”

The same process happens with the other forms of impulsivity. Suppose you abandon a difficult goal the moment you encounter a setback. By quitting, you no longer have to face the possibility of failing, and that relief reinforces the decision to walk away. Your brain begins to conclude that quitting is what protects you from disappointment. Before long, "I'm going to fail anyway" no longer feels like a fear. It feels like an accurate description of who you are.

Next, imagine you lash out at someone or engage in self-harm during an intense emotional moment. The relief that follows reinforces the idea that your emotions are simply too overwhelming to tolerate. Finally, if shopping, drinking, or another risky behavior briefly replaces feelings of emptiness with excitement, you may come to believe that you need those experiences to feel alive.

Changing the Story Changes the Behavior

In a new evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder, we start by uncovering the thinking that powers impulsive actions. Clients are asked to identify the behaviors they use in each of the categories described above: problems making plans, problems following thought, emotion-driven impulses, and sensation seeking. Then, they’re prompted to reflect on why they use that behavior.

Behavior: Binge eating

Because: It helps me numb out when my emotions are too intense

Once those thoughts are brought into awareness, we use cognitive flexibility to ask whether they are the only possible interpretation or whether there might be other possibilities. Are your emotions really too intense to tolerate? Is binge eating the only strategy you can use to cope, or have you just trained yourself to rely on it? You might remind yourself that strong emotions always become less intense over time, even without doing something to push them away.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, simply thinking differently isn't enough to undo years of learning. The brain needs evidence that a different story is true.

New Behaviors Create New Beliefs

Conducting a behavioral experiment allows you to test whether your new way of thinking about the situations that provoke impulsive behavior hold merit. You act as though an alternative explanation might be true and see what happens.

For example, when my clients believe they need the adrenaline of an approaching deadline to get started, I remind them that adrenaline is for lifting cars off of toddlers, not opening a word document. Then, I challenge them to get started on their project early. Specifically, I ask them to set a timer for 5-minutes and work until it goes off. Usually, they persist longer than five minutes because getting started is the hardest part. This experience becomes evidence that they can, in fact, prepare in advance.

This works with other forms of impulsivity. If you believe your emotions are unbearable, you might practice allowing an urge to rise and fall without immediately trying to escape it. And if you've come to rely on shopping, drinking, or other risky behaviors to break through feelings of emptiness, you might try out other, less-damanging activities like making plans with friends or journaling. .

As you collect more evidence, your narrative starts to shift. You are no longer the type of person who needs the pressure of the last minute.

"The Kind of Person You Are"

One of the hardest parts of living with BPD is believing that your patterns define you. But the thoughts that drive impulsive behavior aren't facts. They're learned interpretations. When you begin questioning them and collecting evidence for a different story, impulsive behavior starts to lose its grip.

item.title: Gay Men and Self-Worth: Beyond Visibility and Pride
item.description:
Shame

Gay Men and Self-Worth: Beyond Visibility and Pride

Shame may not be our fault, but healing it is our responsibility.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy shame keeps us connected to empathy and conscience.
  • Worthiness comes from understanding and embracing who we are at our core.
  • Protective silence is the pressure to protect our image by hiding what doesn't show us in a good light.
Source: Hugo Miguel/Unsplash

Not long ago, a friend was traveling and decided to get a haircut at the airport during his layover.

He lives in Los Angeles with his husband, so when the new barber asked him whether he was single or had a wife, he didn’t stop to tell him he’s gay.

It wasn’t that he felt unsafe or worried he could be harmed. He told me it felt easier in the moment to not disrupt the flow of the barber’s heteronormative assumption.

He left feeling disappointed in himself, though, and wondered why, after all this time, it can still sometimes feel easier to hide.

As a means of honoring himself and confronting shame’s lie, he went back to the barbershop after he left and said, “I just wanted to tell you that I’m gay and didn’t say anything before, but I’m happily married and have a loving husband at home in LA.”

In my clinical work with clients, I often hear some version of, “I've done the work, I've come out, I'm successful, and yet I still feel like something's missing.”

While visibility and progress have increased, the inner work of healing shame, internalized homophobia, and spiritual disconnection remains largely unaddressed.

In fact, acknowledging internalized homophobia carries stigma. For gay men, admitting any form of internalized shame can feel like a betrayal of the community, as if by acknowledging it, we're giving credence to the very homophobia we've fought to survive.

Due to stigma, fear of judgment, and a more nuanced dynamic known as protective silence—a pressure to safeguard our image by avoiding narratives that might be seen as “airing our dirty laundry”—many gay men learn to suppress their pain for the sake of collective pride. This can create an inner conflict between honoring our personal experience and staying loyal to the community’s image, where speaking about internalized homophobia feels like exposing a personal failure rather than a shared wound.

Discovering Self-Worth Beyond External Validation

As I began exploring my own incongruence and feelings of unworthiness, I never found anything that addressed self-worth, shame, and spirituality specifically for gay men. What I learned in my own healing, and what I've witnessed in my clients', is worthiness doesn't come from fixing external problems. It comes from understanding and embracing who we are at our core. Not just intellectually, but spiritually.

Internalized homophobia doesn't only affect how we consciously and unconsciously see ourselves. It impacts how we relate to each other as gay men, including our friendships, romantic relationships, sex lives, and coping strategies.

When shame is chronic and internalized, it can lead us to project our unhealed and unconscious shame onto others, specifically other gay men. Because we've disconnected and disowned parts of ourselves we identify as shameful, we might judge each other for being too feminine, too sexual, or too much—when in reality, we’re uncomfortable seeing a part of ourselves reflected back that we haven’t made peace with yet.

Shame can become contagious among gay men, bouncing from one person to the next, disguised as standards or taste or "preference." But underneath, it's a defense mechanism.

Differentiating Between Healthy and Toxic Shame

It’s important to distinguish between healthy shame, which keeps us connected to empathy and conscience, and toxic shame that says, “There’s something wrong with who you are.”

Toxic shame is the spiritual core of internalized homophobia. It’s also why many of us, especially those raised in religious households, become shame-prone. If we were taught our existence was sinful, we learned more than fear of punishment. We internalized a belief that we were fundamentally broken, or worse, that we could go to hell.

Coming out doesn't erase this kind of identity-based trauma. Unhealed wounds live inside our nervous system until we're willing to meet them with compassion and curiosity rather than avoidance.

As a therapist, I talk with clients about how trauma is passed down generationally. If your father had an addiction and it hurt you, it wasn’t your fault. But healing from the pain it caused and how it impacts your life is your responsibility. If we don’t tend to our wounds, we pass them on. The same is true for shame. We may consciously or unconsciously internalize it, but we also have the power to stop passing it on.

For many gay men, our freedom lies in being able to acknowledge how our past still informs our present. Our past lives in our present, and when we choose to transform the present, we make peace with the past.

If I were to ask you where your own sense of worth comes from, whether it's from an achievement, an external marker of success, or something inherent within you, what would you say?

In my forthcoming book, Becoming Worthy: A Gay Man's Guide to Healing Shame and Loving Himself (Bloomsbury, 2027), I explore all of this, including loneliness, religious trauma, body dissatisfaction, and something rarely addressed in books for gay men, our relationship with money.

If any of this resonates, or you have a story of your own you'd like to share, I'd love to hear from you. You can find me on Instagram at @aroadtriptolove, or subscribe below for future posts.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Some Conflicts Never End… and What Actually Changes Them
item.description:
Relationships

Why Some Conflicts Never End… and What Actually Changes Them

Lessons from three decades of studying our hardest disagreements.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Intractable conflicts trap us in binary thinking as situations grow more complex.
  • Framing issues with nuance, not binaries, leads to richer and more productive dialogue.
  • Adaptive conflict responses outperform fixed “style” approaches like chronic cooperation.
  • Conflict isn't the disease, and agreement isn't the cure. The challenge is between rigidity and complexity.
How to find Peace
Source: Photo by Andy Newton on Unsplash

Here's a puzzle I've spent most of my career trying to solve.

About 95% of the conflicts in our lives: with our spouses, coworkers, neighbors, even other nations, eventually get worked out, one way or another. But roughly 5% don't. They grind on for years or decades, consuming everything around them. Mediators fail. Peace deals collapse. Family therapists throw up their hands. And here's the strange part: the harder people try to resolve these conflicts, the more stuck they often become.

For a long time, the field assumed these were simply harder versions of normal disputes: more issues, more history, higher stakes. What my colleagues and I have found, across laboratory studies, organizational research, and analyses of the world's most peaceful societies, is something different. These conflicts aren't harder. They're a different kind of thing entirely.

How Intractable Conflict Simplifies Perception

Watch what happens to people inside a long-running conflict. Objectively, the situation grows more complicated over time: more grievances, more players, more tangled history. But subjectively, something odd occurs: people's experience of the conflict gets simpler. Nuance disappears. There's us and them. Right and wrong. Winning and losing.

I've come to call this the paradox of intractability: as the conflict grows more complex, the mind grows simpler. And that collapse of complexity isn't a side effect, it's the engine. Once everyone involved is thinking in binaries, every new event gets sorted into the same two bins. Every olive branch looks like a trick; every criticism confirms the enemy's malice. The conflict becomes a kind of gravity well. It stops being about anything in particular and starts being the lens through which everything is seen.

This is why well-intentioned interventions so often get swallowed whole. You can't easily argue people out of a pattern, because the pattern is doing their interpreting for them.

What Studies Reveal About Productive Conversations

To study this up close, we built something at Columbia called the Difficult Conversations Lab. We bring in pairs of strangers who genuinely, passionately disagree: about abortion, immigration, the Middle East, and ask them to talk. Then we track everything: what they say, and moment-to-moment, how they feel.

Two findings changed how I think about disagreement.

First, how a topic is framed often matters more than the topic itself. In one experiment, before the conversation, we gave people the same factual information in one of two formats. Half read it as a classic pro-vs-con debate. Half read it as a complicated issue viewed from many angles. That was the only difference, and it changed everything downstream. The "complexity" group thought in more nuanced terms, felt more positive emotion, asked more questions instead of just arguing, and, in one striking result, every single pair in that condition managed to write a joint statement about the problem together, versus fewer than half the pairs in the pro/con condition.

Think about what our information environment feeds us all day: pro versus con, left versus right, hot take versus hot take. We are marinating in the exact format that our data says makes conversations fail.

Second, good conversations aren't nicer, they're richer. When we charted people's emotions over time, the productive conversations weren't the ones free of anger or frustration. They were the ones with a wide, moving range of feeling: irritation giving way to curiosity, tension to laughter, and a favorable overall ratio of positive to negative moments. The failed conversations weren't the angriest ones. They were the stuck ones, flatlined in negativity. Negativity isn't the enemy. Rigidity is.

There is No "Best" Conflict Style

If you've ever taken a workplace assessment that told you your conflict style: collaborator, competitor, avoider, and so on, I have some awkward news from our organizational research: having a style is the problem.

We built an assessment that measures something else: adaptivity, or the capacity to read what a situation actually demands and respond accordingly. Sometimes that means collaborating; sometimes it means standing firm; sometimes it means walking away. Across studies in the U.S. and South Korea, adaptive managers were more satisfied with how conflicts went, felt better at work, and were less likely to want to quit. Chronic cooperators, the people conventional wisdom holds up as the ideal, didn't show the same benefits. Endless cooperation in the face of exploitation isn't virtue; it's a mismatch.

The same principle shows up in our motivation research. You might think effective peacemakers are the optimists, focused on the future we could build. Or maybe the hard-nosed realists, focused on preventing harm. Our experiments found the winner was both at once: what I think of as bifocal vision. "What are we trying to make possible?" and "What must we protect?" are not competing questions. The people who held both did better than those who chose.

A pattern was emerging across every study: in conflict, the healthy state is the more complex one: mixed feelings, multiple strategies, contradictory motives held in tension. Certainty and purity, which feel like strength, are actually symptoms of the trap.

If deep conflicts are self-sustaining patterns, the practical question shifts. Instead of "How do we resolve this dispute?" the question becomes "How do we change the pattern?"

Our research on "ripeness," the conditions under which frozen conflicts finally move, points to a counterintuitive answer. The traditional theory said conflicts resolve when the pain becomes unbearable, so the strategy was pressure: sanctions, stalemates, escalating costs. What we found in studying conflicts that actually transformed is that pain alone rarely does it. What moves people is when an alternative future becomes believable: when a different way of living together becomes visible enough, viable enough, and safe enough to bet on.

That means the work is often indirect. Don't attack the conflict head-on; it will absorb the blow. Instead, strengthen what's already quietly working. Create small, low-risk experiences of a different pattern. Build coalitions broad enough to protect those green shoots. Change the landscape, and the conflict loses its grip.

The last piece of the puzzle came from an unexpected place: societies that don't go to war.

They exist: clusters of neighboring communities, on several continents, that have sustained peace for generations. When we analyzed what sets them apart, the strongest predictors weren't peace treaties or conflict-resolution institutions. They were the everyday stuff: shared norms against fighting, rituals and symbols that make peace socially attractive, identities big enough to hold differences, and webs of economic and social interdependence. And when we modeled how all these factors interact mathematically, we found no single lever: no one fix that produces peace. Peace, it turns out, works exactly like intractable conflict, but in reverse: it's a self-reinforcing pattern, woven from many mutually sustaining strands.

In fact, we can define it with the same math we used in the lab: sustainable peace is a high, stable ratio of positive to negative exchanges between groups. From a twenty-minute conversation between two strangers to centuries of peace between societies, it's the same signature.

Key Takeaways for More Productive Engagement

If there's one idea to take from all this, it's that we've been asking the wrong question. Not "What's the right technique?" but "What's the pattern, and what would change it?"

In your own hardest conflicts, that suggests a different checklist. Notice when your thinking has collapsed into two categories; that's the trap closing, not clarity arriving. Seek out the complicated version of the story before the conversation, not during it. Hold your hopes and your fears at the same time. Stay flexible enough to change your approach when the situation changes. And instead of trying to win the argument, look for one small, credible experience of a better pattern, then protect it.

Conflict isn't the disease, and agreement isn't the cure. The real battle, at every scale, is between rigidity and complexity. Complexity, our data suggests, can win, but only if we stop feeding the machine that makes everything simple.

item.title: What Do Americans Think About?
item.description:
Cognition

What Do Americans Think About?

A new study uses self-reported thought records to analyze what Americans think.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • A new study surveyed 258 Americans using experience sampling for daily updates on their thoughts.
  • Almost half of all thoughts recorded related to bodily signals, work, and food.
  • Cats and dogs were mentioned more than children; and mothers much more than fathers.
Source: Alex Sheldon/Unsplash

A new study, currently in preprint, reports on what Americans think about. Using a technique called the experience sampling method (ESM), the researchers surveyed 258 Americans, who provided the researchers with 23,338 thought record entries. The respondents’ ages ranged from 19 to 71, while 47% were female, 21% were non-white, and education spans ranged from 10 and 21 years.

The respondents would get random notifications by way of an app throughout their days and would then file a thought record based on instructions. Respondents described the thought they were having when they received the notification, and reported:

  • Whether the thought was intrusive or intentional.
  • Which category it applied to, including:
    • Personal care, eat/drink, household activity, purchase, care/help family, care/help non-family, work related, education, civic/clubs, leisure/sports, calls/mail/email, and other.
    • Thought records were analyzed by the researchers for more granularity than these categories.
  • Their happiness at that time, on a 10-point scale.

Given the notifications would come randomly between 7 a.m. and 11 p.m., the researchers could also analyze differences across time of the day. The findings of the study are fascinating and give us great insight into what people think about during their days.

What Did People Think About?

The largest category of thoughts related to senses/percepts—19.1% of thoughts were classed as such—many of which centered on interoceptive sensations, such as thinking about one’s tiredness.

The second most common category was work/job (16.6%), followed by food (14.2%). These three categories accounted for almost half (49.9%) of all thoughts recorded.

The next most popular categories accounted for around one quarter (22.8%) of thoughts: hobbies/games/play/art (10%), relationships/people (9.7%), and health/safety (7.6%).

The remaining categories were chores (6.9%), self-reflection (5.8%), financial/housing/shelter (2.3%), world issues/social issues/politics (3.2%), narratives/stories (2.3%), and music (1.4%).

Interestingly, the authors reported that what people were thinking about predicted momentary happiness more strongly than what they were doing, or characteristics such as demography or socioeconomic status.

Why Were They Thinking These Thoughts?

Among the five causes of thoughts that were self-reported, 41% were reported as intentional (i.e., the person chose to be thinking about x), 31% were self-reported as being due to wandering (cognitively), 27% related to what the person was doing, 15% related to what they were observing or listening to, and 8% were due to being reminded of something. Participants could select multiple choices when classifying these.

In terms of whether participants reported that thoughts were intentional or intrusive, 56% reported intentionality, 23% reported thoughts as being accidental, while 21% were reported as being intrusive.

Source: Sarandy Westfall/Unsplash

Who Were They Thinking About?

In the area of relational thoughts, friend was the most commonly used term. The frequency with which people reported thinking about friends was almost the same as reporting on four romantic relational terms in husband, wife, boyfriend, and girlfriend. Friends were mentioned 4.4 times more than co-workers, though the authors themselves highlight that a friend can be a co-worker, so this might have related more to framing. Altogether, 46% of participants mentioned thinking about friends at least once.

Pets were commonly thought about, with cats and dogs (combined) slightly exceeding the frequency of daughters and sons (combined). It would be important to know if this analysis controlled for whether or not the respondent had children, or was it a case that more participants owned pets, or that participants had more pets than children. Spouses thought of each other, but not as much as they thought of their children. Fathers, sisters, and brothers appeared relatively less than children, while mothers were thought about more than all three combined, and three times more than fathers. Again, analyses here would ideally control for whether one or both parents are alive.

Four Clusters of Thinkers

The authors used cluster analysis to find patterns in thinking styles and reported four clusters:

  1. Worrier—thought about world/political/social issues 60% more, and health/safety 50% more, than the average. Intriguingly, they also listened to music twice as frequently.
  2. Domestic—thought about finances/housing, chores, and narratives/stories around 50% more than average.
  3. Bodily—thought a lot about senses/percepts, tuning into their bodies, around 50% higher than the average. The authors reported this as being 64% female.
  4. Work-hard play-hard—thought about work 50% more than average, and hobbies/games/arts around 25% more, and were 63% male.

Conclusion

The study gives a fascinating insight into day-to-day thinking across a cross-section of Americans over a two-week period. While the broad categories of thinking clusters can be useful initial data, more rigorous research would need to further test this beyond 258 people. As well as more general considerations about the potential weakness of relying on self-report, self-reporting on one’s inner thoughts will likely include a high degree of filtering, if not persona projecting. Shyness, embarrassment, and other self-conscious emotions like guilt would likely play a role. Another consideration lies in type of thinking, with this study seemingly assessing mostly System 2 thinking. Lastly, relying on participants who have been motivated by a financial reward and have been self-selected also tempers generalizability of the findings. With all that said, the study provides useful insights.

item.title: The Therapist Within: An Internal Call to Heal
item.description:
Confidence

The Therapist Within: An Internal Call to Heal

It may be the most important of internal voices.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us have a voice in our heads that functions like an inner therapist.
  • The therapist within tells us to regulate negative feelings, not stuff or suppress them.
  • The therapist within often gets drowned out by conditioned habits of thought and feelings and by bad advice.
  • At the end of the day, the therapist within tells us to live according to our deeper values.

We all have voices within, however faint they may be, left over from parents, teachers, lovers, and, these days, from the Internet. Many of us have a voice that functions like an inner therapist. At its best, this voice reminds us to improve rather than blame, appreciate rather than complain, connect rather than withdraw, and protect people who matter to us. It reminds us to act according to our deeper values instead of temporary feelings. It urges flexibility instead of rigidity and calls us to become the person, partner, parent, and friend we most want to be.

Unfortunately, the therapist within often gets drowned out by conditioned habits of thought and feelings and by bad advice. The adult brain is replete with biases, automatic responses, and habits that can distort judgment. For this reason, we should not place blind trust in every feeling or conclusion that comes to mind. Instead, we must examine evidence for and against our judgments. The ability to question our assumptions is one of the human mind’s greatest strengths.

In an age saturated with self-help advice, this skill has become increasingly important. One sign that we may be consuming too much self-help is the tendency to confuse opinions with scientific findings or to overuse fashionable labels such as “gaslighting,” “narcissist,” “co-dependent,” or “passive aggressive.” Labels oversimplify complex human experiences. Genuine growth comes not from collecting explanations but from testing them. Rather than assuming that a particular interpretation is true, form hypotheses that promote growth and well-being and then evaluate them through your own experience.

The Pain Hypothesis

Emotional pain, like physical pain, evolved to motivate healing, correction, and improvement. Suffering begins when we ignore this motivational signal or replace it with blame, denial, or avoidance. Resentment, anger, contempt, envy, jealousy, and vindictiveness often follow failure to act on pain’s signal to heal and improve. Instead of learning from pain, we become trapped by it.

The signals of emotional pain are within us, although the pain itself is usually stimulated by circumstances and other people. The most common way to alleviate emotional pain is with substances, which always worsen it the next day.

Test the pain hypothesis for yourself. The next time you experience emotional pain, note how you feel when you make efforts to alleviate the causes of it, which are usually a violation of your own values in response to someone else. Ask:

What might I feel guilty about? Ashamed of? Afraid of?

You should notice some amelioration of emotional pain from your efforts to resolve unconscious guilt, shame, and anxiety.

The Healing Power of Emotion Regulation

One of the worst things we can do for mental and physical health is stuff, suppress, or avoid unpleasant feelings. Emotion regulation changes feelings by modifying the meaning we give to our experience. It calms us when upset and cheers us when feeling down.

article continues after advertisement

Emotion regulation is the engine of genuine confidence. Failure and catastrophe occur more often from overconfidence than from under-confidence. Overconfidence underestimates the possibility of failure; under-confidence exaggerates it. Genuine confidence recognizes risks and works to reduce them. True confidence is not certainty; it's realistic preparation. It may be impossible to develop genuine confidence without skill in emotion regulation.

Compassion and Kindness

Emotion regulation is the sustaining force of compassionate and kind behavior. We cannot always generate compassionate feelings on demand, but we can always choose compassionate behavior. We cannot always feel kind, but we can always behave kindly. In fact, feelings follow behavior more than behavior follows feelings. By acting according to our humane values, we’re likely to create the emotional states we seek. For example, if you do not feel loved, make sure that you are loving. Love is not merely something we receive; it is also something we must practice.

The act of giving care, attention, and compassion generates the very sense of connection we long for. People who consistently treat themselves and others with compassion recover more quickly from mistakes, conflicts, and disappointments. Because they respond constructively to suffering, suffering gains less power over their lives.

A Seeming Paradox

There is a seeming paradox at the heart of compassion in relationships. When it’s available whenever needed, it’s seldom needed. Knowing that it’s available when needed reduces the self-doubt that underlies neediness in partners.

The therapist within is not the voice of perfectionism, self-criticism, or endless analysis. It is the voice that calls us back to our values, encourages us to learn from pain, questions our assumptions, and guides us toward growth. It reminds us that well-being is not determined by what we happen to feel at any given moment, but by how consistently we choose to live according to our most humane values.

item.title: Professors Learn Why Education Fails to Restrain Corruption
item.description:
Education

Professors Learn Why Education Fails to Restrain Corruption

Personality, ideology, and opportunity shape corrupt or anti-corrupt intentions.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Personality type and ideology are the primary drivers of the intent to commit or fight corruption.
  • The more authoritarian individuals are, the higher their propensity to engage in corruption.
  • Individuals who believe in the possibility of political change are often the fighters of corruption.
Education doesn't always protect against the slippery slope of norm violations.
Source: Debbie Peterson/Canva

Further education, whether at the university level or as professional ethics training, is thought to curb corruption, but it doesn’t always work. Social psychologists M. Urcia and A. Alva, behavioral economist V. Vivas, and accountant A. Espinosa from three Peruvian universities teamed up to review and test theories of why some highly educated individuals tolerate unethical practices and rationalize corrupt acts. Their research is localized to Peru and generalized to Latin America, but the effects of corruption they outline are universal.

Their 2026 study, “Psychosocial factors associated with corrupt intentions among educated citizens,” assesses 250 Peruvian university students and graduates for associations between political ideology, cynicism, personality, perceptions of ethics norms and political systems, and how these factors influence the response to corruption. They explain that Peruvian university students and graduates understand corruption as a systemic phenomenon that involves citizens through daily practices at a structural, cultural, and direct level.

Their research supports recent findings that personality type and ideology influence perceptions of norms and political systems, leading to cognitive assessments that drive the intent to either tolerate, commit, or fight corruption. They describe the individuals most likely to tolerate or fight corruption, and the societal outcomes of their actions. They note that voluntary compliance with ethical norms relies on perceiving those norms as legitimate and fair. They find one ideology and two personality types are the most likely to lead educated individuals away or toward corruption.

Authoritarianism and Corruption

The more authoritarian individuals are, the higher their propensity to engage in corruption due to a low level of moral indignation about corruption that legitimizes secrecy and lack of transparency as a form of political practice to help authoritarian group members feel secure.

Dark Triad Influence

Individuals with antisocial traits characterized by a lack of empathy, Machiavellianism, and subclinical psychopathy, also known as “Dark Triad” personalities, may use weak norms, moral laxity, and political distrust to normalize and justify corrupt intentions.

When authoritarians, Machiavellians, or subclinical psychopaths perceive that norms are deficient, they create informal or alternative norms or systematically transgress, but do not eliminate norms. They take advantage of deficient and corrupt political systems to achieve pri­vate aims. The resulting social practices demoralize citizens and society. The inequity and injustice arising from the malfunctioning normative system become rationalized as a means of survival in a corrupt environment. Political cynicism arises when the political system is dishonest, immoral, weak, inefficient, unfair, corrupt, limits citizen involvement, fails to represent citizens, is rife with scandals, or violent, and depending on media treatment of these issues, causes widespread distrust. When individuals see low compliance with rules and norms, weak norms, and have low control in their environment, honesty is damaged, and dishonesty becomes positively valued.

Alternative Norms

Alternative norms usually take the form of nepotism and clientelism, a political social system based on an unequal, reciprocal exchange of favors by a powerful figure dispensing benefits—such as government jobs, contracts, or special privilege in exchange for backing, loyalty, or votes.

Alternative norms favor quid-pro-quo, "this for that" transactions in which benefits are distributed based not on public need or merit, but purely as a reward for support. The system often relies on intermediaries or brokers who connect top-level politicians with local voters and involves a relationship where the client depends on the patron's continued power and discretionary control over resources.

How It Impacts Society

Alternative norms significantly skew public resources, undermine the rule of law, reduce meritocracy, and diminish public assets because policymakers favor their cronies over the public interest. Clientelism involves a longer-term, ongoing relationship and functions across multiple government agencies through prevari­cation. Prevaricators skirt the core of an issue to deceive, conceal, or buy time, causing delegitimization and distrust in institutions through deliberate deviation from the truth, evasive speaking, dodging direct questions, or using vague and misleading language. This leads to public confusion and misperceptions of the normative system, such that corrupted systems may be perceived as effective and ethical; and well-func­tioning uncorrupted systems may be perceived as corrupt.

Anti-Corruption Intent

Individuals who hold strong anticorruption intentions perceive norms as unfair or unfulfillable, but believe in the possibility of change, and are confident in institutional reform. Such individuals lose respect for institutional authority when they perceive dysfunction of the justice system, significant systemic ineffectiveness and corruption, and generalized transgression of norms. When they see norms adapting to individual interests, where transgressions are justified because very few controls or sanctions exist, they take on the capacity and responsibility to clean up and improve the political system. This conviction is strengthened by honest, impartial, and trustworthy prosecutors and judiciary. A segment of society characterized by honesty and transparency and in search of change exerts pressure on the political system. However, if this stance of change and intolerance towards corruption is not strong enough, the daily experience with corruption can lead to acceptance of corrupt actions.

The Protective Effect of Education

Higher education does not invariably prevent corrupt intentions when systems are dysfunctional, and corrup­tion is normalized because everyday exposure to corruption erodes intrinsic honesty and undermines the effectiveness of anti-corruption policies. The researchers conclude that education without system legitimacy may be insufficient to curb corrupt intentions.

They explain that when corruption is systemic or has become normalized, even highly educated individuals are constantly faced with the dilemma of tolerate, accommodate, or resist transgressions.

They suggest that if citizens are made more politically aware of the problem of corruption, they will take a greater interest in public affairs, mete out punishment of corrupt officials, and enforce political accountability. The researchers suggest that promoting sophisticated moral reasoning at university level would strengthen citizen commitment and interest and serve as a tool to monitor and control public officials. This includes strengthening the perception that it is possible to reform the political system to serve citizens and is reinforced by greater citizen exposure to effective anticorruption policies and actions.
